newsitem.title: UK: World Cup was political football for Britain.
newsitem.headline: World Cup was political football for Britain.

text.p: England won World Cup glory in 1966 but the soccer tournament turned into a political football for Britain, secret government papers revealed on Wednesday.
England's 1-0 quarter-final defeat of Argentina stirred fiery passions in Buenos Aires while South Korean officials even cheered on North Korea's "giantkiller" team.
England manager Alf Ramsay, whose team finally won the Cup in a thrilling final encounter with West Germany, called the Argentines "animals" after their bruising encounter.
The state papers, finally revealed after 30 years under Britain's stringent secrecy rules, showed how the result sparked outrage in Argentina.
The British embassy received hundreds of abusive calls and jeering youths stormed the British stand at a trade fair. Extra guards were posted at the ambassador's residence.

"Most Argentines quite sincerely believe that the whole tournament was managed, or mismanaged, was a dirty business and a stain on the British reputation for sportsmanship and honesty," the embassy said in a dispatch to London.
North Korea's participation provoked a protest from Seoul. British diplomats agonised on when the North Korean flag should be flown and how often its national anthem should be played.
North Korea defeated Italy to land a place in the quarter finals but then the sigh of relief was almost audible from British officialdom when they were eventually toppled.
"Thank heaven that Portugal finally dispatched the giant killers and we were spared a North Korea/England match," one official said.
But Sir Walter Godfrey, the British ambassador in Seoul, revealed that the South Korean ambassador in London and some of his staff had attended North Korea's matches.
He said the two sides also met unofficially afterwards.
Then the ambassador hastily added with a typical flourish of diplomatic decorum: "None of this is of course known here (in Seoul) and this letter is not for retention."
The combination of sport and royalty also proved to be a diplomatic minefield later in 1966 when Queen Elizabeth's husband, the Duke of Edinburgh, was invited to Argentina for a polo tournament.
Memos flew between ministers as the government puzzled on how to ensure that he did not exceed the 50 pound ($75) spending limit for travel abroad imposed under exchange controls.
The duke, renowned for a string of diplomatic gaffes on tours abroad, was encouraged to cut the trip from six to two weeks and ensure he mixed in some official engagements as well.
Despite the restrictions in austere economic times, officials considered the visit an essential bridge-building exercise after the World Cup debacle.
In 1982, the two countries went to war after Argentina invaded the disputed Falklands and Britain sent a task force to expel them from the South Atlantic islands.
